answer_text:
Under the usual interpretation that “Galois” means over \(\mathbb{Q}\), the smallest such integer is already

\[
\boxed{1}.
\]

In fact, \(\mathbb{Q}(\alpha_n)\) is Galois over \(\mathbb{Q}\) for every \(n\ge 1\).

First identify the nested radicals. We have

\[
\alpha_1=\sqrt{2}=2\cos\frac{\pi}{4}.
\]

Assume

\[
\alpha_{n-1}=2\cos\frac{\pi}{2^n}.
\]

Then

\[
\alpha_n=\sqrt{2+\alpha_{n-1}}
=\sqrt{2+2\cos\frac{\pi}{2^n}}
=\sqrt{4\cos^2\frac{\pi}{2^{n+1}}}
=2\cos\frac{\pi}{2^{n+1}},
\]

where the positive root is taken. Hence

\[
\alpha_n=2\cos\frac{\pi}{2^{n+1}}.
\]

Let

\[
\zeta=e^{2\pi i/2^{n+2}}.
\]

Then

\[
\zeta+\zeta^{-1}=2\cos\frac{\pi}{2^{n+1}}=\alpha_n.
\]

Thus

\[
\mathbb{Q}(\alpha_n)=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta+\zeta^{-1}),
\]

the maximal real subfield of the cyclotomic field \(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta)\). The extension \(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta)/\mathbb{Q}\) is abelian, hence Galois, and its maximal real subfield is the fixed field of complex conjugation. Since the complex-conjugation subgroup is normal, this fixed field is Galois over \(\mathbb{Q}\).

Therefore every \(\mathbb{Q}(\alpha_n)/\mathbb{Q}\) is Galois. In particular, for \(n=1\),

\[
\mathbb{Q}(\alpha_1)=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2}),
\]

which is quadratic and hence Galois. Since no positive integer smaller than \(1\) exists, the smallest such \(n\) is

\[
\boxed{1}.
\]
